A 65-year-old man with a history of hepatitis B, hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity presented with several months of facial swelling, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Shortly thereafter, he developed a pruritic rash on his trunk and upper extremities. He did not report a personal or family history of angioedema. His medications included lisinopril, atorvastatin, albuterol, and ibuprofen for rheumatoid arthritis. The patient had discontinued etanercept six months before presentation. He presented to the emergency department two weeks after seeing his primary care provider for a persistent periorbital, chest, and upper extremity rash. His rash worsened, and he noted new throat swelling and weakness.

Vital signs were stable on arrival. Physical examination was notable for anasarca and a diffuse coalescent erythematous rash over the extremities, chest, and abdomen, with scaling and crusting of the back. There was a heliotrope rash and erythematous lip swelling. He had weakness to resistance in all extremities and a muffled voice without tongue swelling. Over several days, the patient's shoulder and hip weakness progressed, and he could not lift his arms above his head or stand without assistance.

- Laboratory Tests:    - Basic metabolic panel and complete blood count were unremarkable    - Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate    - Negative viral respiratory panel    - C4, C1q, and C1 esterase inhibitor were unremarkable    - Normal serum and urine protein electrophoresis    - Elevated transaminases    - Elevated anti-Sjögren syndrome–related antigen A autoantibodies    - High antinuclear antibody titers    - Negative anti-Jo antibody    - Elevated creatine kinase    - Positive myositis panel for anti-SAE antibodies  - Imaging Studies:    - CT neck: Mild submental inflammatory stranding with no discrete fluid collection or abscess    - Liver ultrasound: Hepatic steatosis    - CT chest: Multiple nodular and airspace opacities, including right lower lobe nodule  - Pathology:    - Skin biopsy results were consistent with Wong-type presentation

A woman in her 50s with a history of chronic pulmonary coccidiomycosis being treated with fluconazole was admitted for fever, hypotension, and rash. Three months prior, pembrolizumab treatment was stopped because of a widespread morbilliform reaction, which had resolved completely 6 to 8 weeks before admission. The new widespread, asymptomatic skin eruption had been ongoing for 1 to 2 weeks and appeared different from her previous reaction.

Total body skin examination findings were notable for widespread, nontender, erythematous patches and thin plaques, some with prominent overlying telangiectases and hyperpigmentation.

- Laboratory tests: Complete blood cell count showed white blood cell count of 4100/μL, absolute neutrophil count of 2940/μL, hemoglobin level of 8.2 g/dL, and platelet count of 62 ×103/μL. Blood culture results showed no growth at 1 week. Serum β-D-glucan, galactomannan, Coccidioides antibody by complement fixation, and immunodiffusion results were negative. Respiratory viral panel and SARS-CoV-2 test results were negative.- Pathology:   Image Title: Skin Biopsy Findings  Image Description: Hematoxylin-eosin stained sections and CD56 immunostaining showing intravascular atypical cells.- Additional Tests:  - Brain MRI performed  - Lumbar puncture performed  - Bone marrow biopsy performed

clinical_record:
A woman in her 80s with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney disease presented with purpuric lesions on her face, elbows, knees, and feet. She was initially admitted for altered mental status in the setting of an unwitnessed fall and was noted to have 'bruises' on her lower extremities. New lesions developed on her nose, ear, and the extensor surfaces of her arms bilaterally.

The patient's nose, bilateral cheeks, forehead, and left ear (helical rim and antihelix) were found to have dusky purpuric macules and patches. Her knees, feet, and the extensor surfaces of her arms had reticulated purpuric macules and patches. There was skin sloughing off the lesions on her elbows and knees.

- Laboratory tests:     - Hypercalcemia (calcium level, 11.5 mg/dL)    - Acute kidney injury (creatinine level, 5.6 mg/dL)    - Rouleaux and cryoprotein precipitate on peripheral blood smear    - Abnormal paraprotein band on serum and urine protein electrophoreses    - Monoclonal IgG-κ protein on immunofixation electrophoresis    - Elevated serum cryoglobulin levels (cryocrit, 16%)    - Negative results for hepatitis, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies  - Biopsy findings:    Four-millimeter punch biopsy specimens from left ear, right arm, and forehead showed multifocal intravascular fibrinoid material consisting of a mix of cryoglobulins and fibrin thrombi with relatively little vessel wall inflammation  - Imaging studies:    CT scan of pelvis revealed lytic bony lesions      - Bone marrow biopsy:    Hypercellular marrow consisting of 80% plasma cells with atypical morphology and κ-light-chain restriction

clinical_record:
An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.
